conventions.convention: Treatment versions form a nonempty countable discrete set and specify intervention protocols. Consistency means Y = Y^A almost surely; interference must be incorporated into the specified intervention version.

Positivity for a treatment value requires positive marginal treatment probability and a strictly positive conditional treatment probability almost surely under the target covariate law. No uniform positive lower bound is required.

Conditional exchangeability is joint conditional independence of the sigma-algebra generated by the entire potential-outcome family and the treatment sigma-algebra, given the baseline covariate sigma-algebra.

ATE uses the treatment-1 minus treatment-0 orientation with both potential outcomes integrable. CATE is an almost-sure conditional-expectation class, without specified values at null covariate values.

The identification theorem assumes AC and standard-Borel covariates. It constructs the outcome regression under the probability law conditional on the treatment atom, zero-fills nonintegrable kernel sections, and identifies the resulting regression only almost everywhere under the target covariate law.
Integrability is required for each potential outcome under consideration; global integrability of the observed outcome across all treatment arms is not assumed.

load_bearing.statement: Under AC, countably discrete treatment versions containing 0 and 1, standard-Borel covariates, consistency, joint conditional exchangeability, and positivity for each treatment a under consideration with Y^a integrable, the treatment-stratum conditional regression m_a is target-covariate integrable, uniquely determined almost everywhere by the observed law, and E[Y^a] = ∫m_a dP_L. With both binary levels satisfying these hypotheses, m_1 − m_0 represents CATE and its integral is ATE; the potential-outcome means and ATE are identifiable.

Assume AC. If U is real integrable and conditionally independent of the random element Z given a sub-sigma-algebra G in the bounded-function sense, then for every bounded measurable real h, E[U h(Z) | G] = E[U | G] E[h(Z) | G] almost surely.
Conditional exchangeability given L means σ(Y^a : a ∈ A) ⊥ σ(A) given σ(L), using bounded-measurable-function conditional factorization under AC.
Positivity for a on the target population means both P(A=a)>0 and E[1_{A=a} | σ(L)]>0 almost surely under the target law of L; every treatment value in a contrast must satisfy it.

seams_checked.note: Backdoor and front-door statements use structural potential outcomes and factual consistency compatibly with the assigned definition. Their atomic-treatment support and conditional-kernel qualifications preserve the relevant conventions. They supply their own graphical arguments rather than invoking joint exchangeability from this batch without proof.

Standardization explicitly preserves the earlier theorem's countably discrete treatment, standard-Borel covariate, AC, integrability, consistency, full-family exchangeability, and positivity hypotheses on their overlapping domain. Its arbitrary-covariate and general target-atom extensions have separate arguments. IPW preserves the same full-family convention and explicitly distinguishes its atom-specific extension.

This is a contextual page prerequisite rather than a direct citation of an assigned item. The IV definitions use compatible treatment-version, consistency, and treatment-1 minus treatment-0 ATE conventions. Instrument independence is stated separately from treatment exchangeability, and the LATE theorem does not identify LATE with population ATE.

Mediation definitions retain specified treatment versions, target-population contrasts, the binary ATE orientation, and target-law treatment positivity. Joint intervention and nested counterfactual semantics are supplied by the SCM definitions. The identification theorem explicitly adds independent-error structure, cross-world restrictions, mediator support domination, and integrability.
